lesson.title: Mapping Genes by Counting Crossovers
lesson.summary: Recombination frequency is the percentage of offspring with new allele combinations produced by crossing over, and it gives geneticists a way to estimate how far apart two linked genes sit on a chromosome.
lesson.body:
In the previous chapter, a test cross between a fly heterozygous for body color and wing shape and a fully recessive fly produced 1000 offspring: 440 parental AaBb, 440 parental aabb, 60 recombinant Aabb, and 60 recombinant aaBb. Genetic linkage explained why the parental classes so heavily outnumbered the recombinant classes. Recombination frequency turns that observation into a number.

Recombination frequency, abbreviated RF, is calculated as the number of recombinant offspring divided by the total number of offspring, multiplied by 100 percent. Using the numbers above, the total number of recombinants is 60 plus 60, which equals 120. Dividing by the total offspring, 120 divided by 1000 equals 0.12, and multiplying by 100 percent gives an RF of 12 percent. That single number condenses the whole cross into a measurement of how often a crossover occurred between the two genes.

Why does this percentage tell us about distance along the chromosome. Crossing over is a physical, roughly random event that can happen anywhere along the length of a paired chromosome. The farther apart two genes are, the more physical space lies between them, and the more likely it is that a crossover will land somewhere in that stretch and separate the alleles. Genes that sit right next to each other have very little space between them for a crossover to occur, so they show a low RF and stay tightly linked. Genes that sit farther apart on the same chromosome show a higher RF, because there is more opportunity for a crossover to fall between them. This proportional relationship is the basis of genetic mapping: an RF of 1 percent is defined as one map unit, also called one centimorgan, so an RF of 12 percent corresponds to a map distance of about 12 map units between the body color and wing shape genes.

The relationship has limits worth knowing. As two genes get farther and farther apart on the same chromosome, multiple crossovers can occur between them, and some of those crossovers cancel each other out, restoring a parental combination even though the genes are far apart. Because of this, RF values level off and approach a maximum of about 50 percent for genes that are very far apart on the same chromosome, which looks statistically identical to independent assortment, even though the genes are technically still linked. In other words, an RF near 50 percent cannot distinguish between two genes that are extremely far apart on the same chromosome and two genes on entirely different chromosomes. An RF well below 50 percent, like the 12 percent calculated above, is what allows geneticists to confidently say two genes are linked and to estimate roughly how far apart they sit.
